question: Has road safety for pedestrians in Brooklyn gotten better since 2013? Make a chart suitable for a local news story and summarize the findings.

options.metric: Annual number of pedestrians injured in police-reported Brooklyn crashes
options.reason: Injury counts show the annual burden of nonfatal pedestrian harm in an intuitive, locally relevant measure.
options.answer: Pedestrian injuries fell from 3,641 in 2013 to 2,835 in 2025 (22.1% lower), though the count has risen each year since 2021.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether the number of pedestrians injured in Brooklyn crashes is lower than in 2013: it is, despite a steady increase since 2021. Injury counts are a defensible measure of common harm, but this chart leaves deaths and changes in the amount of walking unaccounted for; it cannot establish risk per pedestrian trip or mile.

options.metric: Annual number of pedestrians killed in police-reported Brooklyn crashes
options.reason: Fatalities capture the most severe road-safety outcome and should be considered alongside injury counts.
options.answer: Pedestrian deaths increased from 30 in 2013 to 39 in 2025 (30.0% higher), with substantial year-to-year variation.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether the most severe recorded outcome improved: pedestrian deaths were higher in 2025 than in 2013. Fatality counts are a direct measure of lethal harm, but this chart leaves nonfatal injuries and pedestrian exposure unaccounted for, so it cannot establish fatality risk per trip or mile walked.

answer:
Reported pedestrian injuries in Brooklyn were 22% lower in 2025 than in 2013—2,835 versus 3,641—but have risen each year since 2021; these counts aren’t adjusted for pedestrian exposure.
Pedestrian deaths were 30% higher in 2025 than in 2013—39 versus 30—with substantial year-to-year variation.
